e: A NAT gateway in a public subnet, with the private subnet's default route pointing to it, allows outbound internet access (such as downloading updates) without allowing inbound connections from the internet. An internet gateway route in a private subnet makes it public, and a NAT instance must be in a public subnet.

Amazon EFS is a shared file system that multiple EC2 instances can access at the same time, grows automatically, and stores data redundantly across AZs. EBS attaches to one instance (in one AZ), Glacier Deep Archive isn't for active access, and AWS Backup isn't a primary store.

Policy 1 allows ec2:* (plus read-only IAM, KMS list, and logs get/describe actions, and ds:*). Policy 2 explicitly denies ds:Delete*. So the engineer can delete EC2 instances, cannot delete directories (explicit deny), can't delete IAM users (only Get/List allowed), and can't delete CloudWatch logs (only Get/Describe).

Referencing security group IDs as the source or destination in rules restricts traffic to members of the specific tier's group, applying least privilege and adapting as instances change. Instance IDs aren't valid in rules, and CIDR blocks of the VPC or subnets are far broader.

Store the order first, then send its order number to an SQS FIFO queue. FIFO provides ordering and deduplication, so resubmissions don't create duplicate processing, and the payment service deletes the message after processing. SNS and Firehose don't provide this queuing and exactly-once behavior.

Versioning keeps all versions of documents so overwrites and deletes can be recovered, and MFA Delete adds protection against permanent or accidental deletion of versions. A read-only ACL would stop users from uploading, and IAM policies or KMS encryption don't address versions or accidental deletion.

A CloudWatch metric stream sends Auto Scaling metrics in near real time to Kinesis Data Firehose, which delivers them to S3 with no servers and no effect on instance launches. EMR is not serverless, scheduled Lambda isn't near real time, and bootstrapping agents on instances slows launches.

A Glue ETL job natively converts CSV to Parquet at scale, and a Lambda function triggered by S3 PUT events starts the job, so there is no cluster to manage. Lambda alone struggles with 1 GB files, and managing Spark jobs yourself or Athena-based conversion adds work.

AWS Backup provides managed, consistent, restorable RDS backups with a daily schedule and a 2-year retention in a backup vault, with centralized management. RDS automated backups are limited to 35 days, and DLM, CloudWatch Logs, or DMS aren't proper backup mechanisms.

Join the FSx for Windows File Server file system to the Active Directory, so the on-premises AD users and groups control access to shares, folders, and files using Windows ACLs. IAM groups and tags don't control SMB file permissions.

CloudFront can cache different versions of content based on request headers such as device type, and a Lambda@Edge function can inspect the User-Agent header to serve device-specific objects. NLBs and Global Accelerator don't do host or path-based routing by device.

VPC peering is the cheapest way to connect the VPCs in the same Region, with route entries in both VPCs and an ElastiCache security group rule allowing the application's security group. A transit VPC adds cost and complexity, and peering connections don't have security groups.

An ECS cluster with the Fargate launch type runs containers without managing servers and scales automatically, and a desired task count of at least 2 provides availability. EC2 launch types and self-managed Kubernetes require managing infrastructure.

An ALB performs health checks and only routes to healthy instances, and Route 53 points to the ALB, so DNS never returns an unhealthy instance's IP. Route 53 simple or failover records for each instance still return IPs of unhealthy instances or aren't suited here, and CloudFront doesn't solve it.

CloudFront delivers HTTPS content from the edge, and keeping the EC2 instances in private subnets behind a public ALB (the origin) limits exposure, which is the most secure design. Instances in public subnets or used directly as origins are more exposed.

Global Accelerator continuously health-checks Regional endpoints (the ALBs) and routes users to the closest healthy one over the AWS global network, giving low latency and automatic failover. CloudFront with S3 or DynamoDB DAX don't monitor and redirect between Regional application endpoints.

Kinesis Data Firehose ingests data in near real time, encrypts it, and converts it to Parquet while storing in S3, and Kinesis Data Analytics analyzes the streaming data, all managed. EMR clusters or custom Lambda glue add operational overhead.

An ElastiCache layer in front of the database serves frequent read requests (like score displays) from memory, reducing database read load with few architecture changes. RDS Proxy manages connections but doesn't reduce reads, and migrating to Lambda or DynamoDB means big changes.

A read replica offloads the analysts' read-only queries from the primary database, with minimal changes to the application. Exporting to DynamoDB, ElastiCache, or Redshift involves more work and data pipelines.

Client-side encryption encrypts the data before it's uploaded, satisfying 'encrypted at rest before upload', and using HTTPS covers in-transit encryption. Server-side encryption, bucket policies, or default bucket encryption encrypt data only after it reaches S3.

Because the peak is predictable and the job starts at 1 AM each night, a scheduled scaling action can raise capacity shortly before the batch job and scale back down afterward, so capacity is ready quickly at low cost. Changing min/max or step size doesn't pre-provision capacity.

CloudFront in front of the ALB caches and accelerates the dynamic website from edge locations worldwide, and caching based on the Accept-Language header serves each language version without recreating the architecture in more Regions. An S3-only site can't serve a dynamic site, and API Gateway or NGINX caches add complexity.

Aurora global database replicates to the DR Region with typically under a second of lag, and a warm standby (a scaled-down, always running copy of the environment) has a lower RTO than pilot light because it can take traffic right away and just scale up. RDS Multi-AZ doesn't replicate across Regions.

Copying AMIs to a second Region and using CloudFormation to automatically deploy the infrastructure there during a disaster meets an RTO under 4 hours while keeping almost nothing running during normal operation. Keeping active instances costs more, and custom Lambda scripts are less maintainable than CloudFormation.

Usage is predictable: a scheduled action that raises desired capacity to 20 shortly before the office opens ensures instances are ready at the start of the day. Dynamic scaling reacts too late, and setting minimum and maximum to 20 would prevent scaling down and cost more.
